models.collectorNote: Donohue editions and 401 cars lead; Pierre Cardin interiors are the conversation piece that keeps climbing. Undervalued next to Mustang and Camaro equivalents, for now.

generations.name: Javelin (first generation)
generations.note: Sixes to the 390 V8; the 1970 Mark Donohue edition marked AMC's Trans-Am push with a ducktail spoiler and the 360 or 390 under the hood.

generations.name: Javelin (second generation)
generations.note: Bigger, curvier, with flared arches and the 401 V8 on top. Roger Penske's team took the Trans-Am title in 1971 and 1972; the Pierre Cardin interior option remains the strangest entry on any muscle-era option sheet.

models.intro: AMC's pony car, and a good one: styled by Dick Teague, raced by Penske, and armed with engines up to the 401. The second-generation car won the Trans-Am championship outright in 1971 and 1972.

models.collectorNote: Two seats, real rarity, and muscle-era pace: Big Bad colour cars (orange, green, blue) draw the eye and the bids. Verify the 390 is born-with, not swapped in.

generations.name: AMX
generations.note: About 19,000 built across three years. The 390 with the Go-Package, discs, handling kit, stripes, is the spec; Hurst's SS drag cars are the unicorns.

models.intro: America's other two-seat sports car: a Javelin with a foot cut out of the wheelbase, a 390 V8 option, and a name made of the company's initials. Craig Breedlove took one to Bonneville records before it even went on sale.

models.collectorNote: Seventies kitsch with a rising floor. V8 and Levi's cars are the collectible ones; originality beats restoration at these values.

generations.name: Gremlin
generations.note: Over 670,000 built. Sixes did the volume; the 5.0 V8 made it a stoplight surprise, and the 1977 Gremlin X kept the stripes honest. Levi's denim interiors were a real option.

models.intro: Introduced on April Fool's Day, 1970, a Rambler American with the back chopped off, styled on an air-sickness bag according to legend. Cheap, cheeky, and with the optional 304 V8, absurdly quick for a subcompact.

models.collectorNote: Pure nostalgia economics: tidy survivors are cheap fun, and the film car aura guarantees thumbs-ups per mile like nothing else at the price.

generations.name: Pacer
generations.note: Six-cylinder power only at first; a 304 V8 arrived for 1978. The cab-forward glasshouse anticipated modern packaging by a decade, even if the car around it stayed seventies.

models.intro: The wide small car: as broad as a full-size sedan, glass everywhere, and one door longer than the other so rear passengers could climb in. Designed for a rotary engine GM cancelled, immortalised by Wayne's World.

models.collectorNote: Wagons lead a small, devoted market. Rust and tired AWD viscous couplings are the checks; good ones are appreciating as the crossover's origin story gets retold.

generations.name: Eagle / SX/4 / Kammback
generations.note: The wagon is the icon, woodgrain optional, dignity intact. The 4.2 six and full-time AWD made it the ski-town and rural-route default of the eighties; the line outlived AMC itself by a model year.

models.intro: The crossover, invented fifteen years early: a Concord body on full-time all-wheel drive with raised suspension, in wagon, sedan, coupe and the SX/4 hatch. Subaru and every modern crossover owe it a footnote at least.
